newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian demand for thermal, steam coal shooting up.
newsitem.headline: Asian demand for thermal, steam coal shooting up.

text.p: Asian demand for thermal and steam coal will rise sharply by the turn of the century and may even outstrip supply, industry and shipping analysts said on Thursday.

Demand for coal, most of which will go into power projects to supply electricity to the region's rapidly growing economies, will also put pressure on available shipping in the area, the analysts said at the start of the 5th International Bulk Congress in Singapore.

"It is obvious that Asian thermal coal demand will grow strongly over the next six years at a rate likely to exceed the ability of coal producers to supply," Graeme Robertson, chairman and chief executive officer of the Swabara Group in Indonesia, said in a speech to the conference.
"The balance of supply and demand will become very delicate with pressure on coal prices by consumers to ensure stable deliveries," he added.
Thermal coal imports in Asia are likely to rise to 250.6 million tonnes in 2002 from an estimated 139.2 million tonnes in 1996, Robertson said.

Robin Thomas, an analyst for London-based shipbrokers Simpson, Spence and Young, said steam coal imports in the Asia-Pacific would rise to 190.6 million tonnes by 2000 from an estimate of 136.4 million tonnes in 1996.

The construction of power plants from India to the Philippines for electricity generation may spike demand higher. "Even if only a proportion of independent power project (IPP) capacity comes on-line, these indicative figures for steam coal demand could significantly alter the global steam coal trade during the next 10 years, especially in the Asia-Pacific region," Thomas said.
Robertson, who is also a director of the World Coal Institute, said China alone planned to expand coal-fired power capacity to 230,000 megawatts by 2002 from 100,000 megawatts in 1993.
In India, coal demand for power generation would hit 330 million tonnes in 2002 while available domestic supplies would only reach 300 million tonnes.
Demand in other countries like South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines was likewise accelerating.

"Asian coal imports have increased by 38.5 percent in the last four years and I don't forsee any likelihood of this trend abating very significantly," Bruce Farthing, consultant director of the International Associationn of Dry Cargo Shipowners (Intercargo), said at the conference.
Robertson said tight supplies of coal would encourage new coal mining development in Australia and Indonesia.

He said a tight demand/supply relationship in the future would open the Asian coal trade to lower heating value sub-bituminous coal, such as from Powder River basin in the U.S. and the Surat Basin in Queensland. Currently, sub-bituminous coal is less economic and requires high infrastructure investment.
He said the shipping industry may benefit from brisk demand through strong freight rates.

"(But) the pace of development of these new markets will also depend on investment in ports and associated infrastructure," he said. "Bulk handling equipment manufacturers and port developers/operators will benefit from coastal IPPs constructing dedicated unloading facilities."
